title: Why Fetch When You Can Sync? Building Local-First Apps on a Sync Engine Architecture
gist: ElectricSQL CEO James Arthur argues sync-based, reactive client-server data binding is the next frontier past exhausted client-side reactivity, and shows how Electric's read-path sync engine plus the vendor-agnostic TanStack DB client (now with query-driven, on-demand sync) lets teams incrementally adopt local-first architecture on existing infrastructure instead of the greenfield, lock-in-heavy sync platforms that came before.

themes.theme: Sync as the next frontier for frontend and agentic apps

insights.claim: Arthur argues the remaining 'alpha' in client-side reactivity frameworks (signals, actions, reducers) is largely exhausted, and the real frontier is extending reactivity to the server — replacing imperative data fetching with declarative sync-based data bindings across the whole stack.
insights.speaker: James Arthur
insights.so_what: Frames sync-engine architecture, not further client-state-management innovation, as the next place to look for meaningful frontend performance and DX gains.
insights.quote: If you see a gap that exists and you no longer go for it, then you are no longer a racing driver.
insights.locator: There's a quote from the racing driver Ayrton Senna

insights.claim: As agentic systems put multiple users, agents, and spawned sub-agents all writing data on the server simultaneously, Arthur argues sync-based reactive state management becomes a necessity rather than an option, since polling for every actor's changes does not scale.
insights.speaker: James Arthur
insights.so_what: Positions sync-engine adoption as a prerequisite architecture for products building multi-agent, human-in-the-loop workflows, not just a UX nicety for traditional apps.
insights.quote: You need a reactive data plane to be able to keep users and agents in sync in this next generation of software, which means by definition that you need reactive state management that extends across client and server.
insights.locator: Particularly with agents, there's now loads more going on on the server

insights.claim: Arthur argues LLM-generated code using imperative data fetching quickly becomes unmanageable because the model cannot control what network requests happen where as the app renders, whereas declarative sync-based data bindings let the underlying system handle data transfer and placement, allowing LLM-written code to scale into production.
insights.speaker: James Arthur
insights.so_what: Suggests sync-based architectures are specifically better suited to AI-coding-agent-generated frontends than the fetch-based patterns most LLMs currently default to.
insights.locator: If the coding agents are writing code like this

themes.theme: Why sync engines weren't mainstream until now

insights.claim: Reference applications built on sync engines (Figma, Linear, Notion, and internally at Meta) required millions of dollars of engineering investment from elite teams, historically pricing sync-engine architecture out of reach for most product teams and keeping HTTP-based fetching the default.
insights.speaker: James Arthur
insights.so_what: Explains the historical cost barrier that off-the-shelf sync engines are now trying to remove, useful context for evaluating whether a vendor's tooling has actually closed that gap.
insights.locator: All these reference apps like Figma, like Linear, like Notion

insights.claim: Arthur frames the sync-architecture choice as an 'innovation token' trade-off: HTTP requests are stateless, easy to deploy, instrument, and debug, while WebSockets carry state on the server side of the connection that is harder to scale and debug — explaining why most teams have historically and rationally avoided real-time sync architectures despite the UX upside.
insights.speaker: James Arthur
insights.so_what: A reusable decision framework for evaluating any new stateful protocol adoption: weigh the UX gain against the operational debugging and scaling cost.
insights.locator: If you just look at it operationally, an HTTP request is stateless

insights.claim: A range of off-the-shelf sync-engine products already exists (Convex, Ditto, Instant, LiveStore, Jazz, PowerSync, RxDB, Zero/Replicache from Rocicorp), but each requires adopting an opinionated greenfield stack, creating vendor lock-in that teams with existing systems or infrastructure preferences often cannot or will not accept.
insights.speaker: James Arthur
insights.so_what: A competitive map of the sync-engine market and its shared weakness (lock-in) that any vendor-neutral entrant, including Electric, is explicitly trying to exploit.
insights.quote: Vercel is a super compelling platform, but it is also a Faustian pact.
insights.locator: Like we were looking at Vercel earlier

insights.claim: Electric's sync engine performs read-path sync with partial replication and fan-out, delivering data through a standard HTTP protocol that runs over existing CDN infrastructure like Cloudflare and Fastly, and works against any standard Postgres database with logical replication enabled, hosted anywhere (AWS, Neon, Supabase, or self-managed).
insights.speaker: James Arthur
insights.so_what: Signals Electric is built to slot into existing infrastructure (CDN, standard Postgres) rather than require a new backend, differentiating it from the greenfield-stack competitors listed earlier.

insights.claim: TanStack DB is a roughly 20-kilobyte, vendor-agnostic JavaScript client-side reactive database — not a multi-megabyte WASM download — stewarded by the TanStack open-source project (about 30 maintainers, not owned by one company, led by Tanner Linsley), which has passed 4 billion downloads and is described as roughly the second most popular app-development framework after Next.js.
insights.speaker: James Arthur
insights.so_what: TanStack's existing scale (4B+ downloads, #2 framework by the presenter's account) gives query-driven sync a large pre-existing distribution channel, relevant to how fast this pattern could spread.
insights.locator: TanStack is a very popular infra-vendor agnostic

insights.claim: TanStack DB is designed for incremental adoption: existing React Query-based applications can migrate one root or component at a time, progressing from pure API-query apps to query-based TanStack DB collections to fully sync-based Electric-backed collections, without requiring a full rewrite.
insights.speaker: James Arthur
insights.so_what: Lowers the adoption barrier for teams with existing React Query codebases, directly addressing the lock-in and all-or-nothing rewrite objections raised against competing sync engines.
insights.locator: The key idea is that it allows you to incrementally migrate existing cloud-first applications

insights.claim: TanStack DB's live queries run on a TypeScript implementation of differential dataflow, propagating only data deltas when changes occur rather than re-running full queries, keeping complex multi-join, multi-aggregate queries across many components rendering within a single animation frame instead of degrading to hundreds of milliseconds as component count grows.
insights.speaker: James Arthur
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific mechanism (delta propagation via differential dataflow) behind TanStack DB's sub-millisecond query claims, useful for technically evaluating it against alternative client-side query engines.
insights.locator: the query engine is based on a TypeScript implementation of differential dataflow

themes.theme: Query-driven sync as a step-change capability

insights.claim: TanStack DB's newest capability, query-driven sync (enabled via syncMode: 'on-demand'), pushes live-query predicates from component code (such as a project ID) down to the collection at runtime, dynamically syncing only the additional data subset needed rather than requiring the whole authorized dataset to be synced upfront.
insights.speaker: James Arthur
insights.so_what: Directly solves the data-loading scaling problem (e.g., not syncing all 35,000 issues in a large tracker at once) that had been the main practical objection to sync-everything architectures.
insights.locator: TanStack DB now supports query-driven sync

insights.claim: Query-driven sync drew public endorsement from prominent developers — Joe Savona of Meta's React/Relay team called it 'kicking myself we didn't build it' good, and Arthur reports TanStack's own Tanner Linsley described it as what he only dreamed of when he started building React Query.
insights.speaker: James Arthur
insights.so_what: Notable third-party technical validation, though it is secondhand social-media reaction cited by Electric's own CEO and should be weighed as such rather than independent benchmarking.
insights.quote: This is 'kicking myself we didn't build it' good.
insights.locator: You don't have to take my word for it. Just under that tweet, that's Joe Savona

insights.claim: In a live demo on a 500,000-row issue-tracker dataset ('LinearLarge'), the sync-based app loaded instantly by fetching only a small initial subset and filling in additional rows on demand as the user scrolled or changed filters, versus what Arthur says would normally take 10-20 seconds to load that volume of data directly from a database.
insights.speaker: James Arthur
insights.so_what: An illustrative vendor demo of query-driven sync's practical effect at scale; useful as a directional signal but not an independently verified benchmark.

themes.theme: Design philosophy: read-path sync generalized, write-path left flexible

insights.claim: Electric deliberately scopes itself to read-path sync only, treating write-path sync as too solution-specific to generalize — after an earlier attempt to build comprehensive write-path guarantees (finality of local writes, referential integrity) proved too complex, the product instead lets each application choose its own write-back strategy while tying into Electric's optimistic-state machinery via transaction ID matching.
insights.speaker: James Arthur
insights.so_what: A reusable design principle for infrastructure builders: standardize the part of a hard problem that generalizes well (reads) and deliberately leave the part that doesn't (writes) to the application, rather than over-engineering a one-size-fits-all solution.
insights.locator: Read-path synchronization is something every app needs

insights.claim: For applications that do need concurrent-editing conflict resolution, Electric and TanStack DB support CRDT-based approaches at the data-model level, including Yjs and Automerge integrations and pg_crdt inside Postgres, but Arthur argues the vast majority of applications don't need this complexity and should default to simple server-authoritative writes with rollback.
insights.speaker: James Arthur
insights.so_what: Gives teams a decision rule: only reach for CRDTs when building genuinely low-latency, real-time collaborative editing (e.g., text editors), not as a default for typical CRUD apps.
insights.locator: I think one of the realities around this is that for most applications

insights.claim: Electric built PGlite, a version of Postgres that runs in the browser, with a sync adapter supporting synchronization of multiple shapes to multiple tables at once, specifically for applications that need true referential integrity across concurrently syncing data streams.
insights.speaker: James Arthur
insights.so_what: A specific tool (PGlite) worth evaluating for teams that need stronger cross-table consistency guarantees than TanStack DB's default join behavior provides.
insights.locator: We also developed this project called PGlite

themes.theme: Delivery mechanism: long polling over WebSockets

insights.claim: Electric deliberately built its sync protocol on long polling rather than WebSockets so data delivery could run through standard CDN infrastructure; this enables 'request coalescing,' where many clients subscribed to the same URL (e.g., everyone in the same workspace) collapse into a single request to the origin server, offloading traffic from the sync service.
insights.speaker: James Arthur
insights.so_what: A counterintuitive infrastructure choice — long polling over WebSockets — that trades a marginal per-connection latency cost for CDN-scale cacheability, statelessness, and easier operational scaling, a pattern other real-time systems could copy.
insights.locator: We deliberately built an old-fashioned long polling-based protocol

insights.claim: For latency-sensitive cases like token streaming or presence, Electric can switch a stream to server-side events (SSE) mode within the same stateless HTTP-based protocol, avoiding the buffering overhead that comes from long-polling reconnects on high-frequency small messages.
insights.speaker: James Arthur
insights.so_what: Shows the architecture has a specific escape hatch for high-frequency streaming use cases (like token-by-token LLM output) without abandoning the CDN-friendly stateless design.
insights.locator: Electric also supports a server-side events mode

themes.theme: Referential integrity trade-offs across sync streams

insights.claim: TanStack DB has no formal concept of referential integrity for synced collections, so a live-query join simply won't match if related data (e.g., a comment before its parent blog post) hasn't finished syncing yet — a trade-off Arthur frames as a feature, since it sidesteps most of the complexity normally needed to enforce foreign-key constraints across independently syncing streams.
insights.speaker: James Arthur
insights.so_what: A specific, non-obvious consistency trade-off to understand before adopting this architecture for data models with strict cross-table integrity requirements.
insights.locator: TanStack DB as a client store doesn't have any formal concept of referential integrity
